name: Equiano on how wars and kidnapping fed the slave trade
text: From what I can recollect of these battles, they appear to have been irruptions of one little state or district on the other, to obtain prisoners or booty. Perhaps they were incited to this by those traders who brought the European goods I mentioned amongst us. Such a mode of obtaining slaves in Africa is common; and I believe more are procured this way, and by kidnapping, than any other[E]. When a trader wants slaves, he applies to a chief for them, and tempts him with his wares. It is not extraordinary, if on this occasion he yields to the temptation with as little firmness, and accepts the price of his fellow creatures liberty with as little reluctance as the enlightened merchant. Accordingly he falls on his neighbours, and a desperate battle ensues.
author: Olaudah Equiano
witness: Written in London in 1789 by a formerly enslaved man for a British abolitionist public, at the height of the petition campaign. Equiano says he was born in Igboland and kidnapped as a child; Vincent Carretta has found records suggesting a birth in South Carolina, so the African chapters may draw on others’ memories. Read it as an informed African abolitionist’s analysis, written to persuade.

name: Equiano on the hold of a slave ship
text: The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us. This produced copious perspirations, so that the air soon became unfit for respiration, from a variety of loathsome smells, and brought on a sickness among the slaves, of which many died, thus falling victims to the improvident avarice, as I may call it, of their purchasers.
author: Olaudah Equiano
witness: An abolitionist text of 1789 describing a voyage of the 1750s, published when Parliament was hearing evidence on shipboard conditions. Whatever his birthplace, the conditions he describes match surgeons’ testimony and the voyage data; the language is shaped for a British reader.

name: Las Casas on the destruction of Hispaniola’s people
text: first assaulted the innocent Sheep, so qualified by the Almighty, as is premention'd, like most cruel Tygers, Wolves and Lions hunger-starv'd, studying nothing, for the space of Forty Years, after their first landing, but the Massacre of these Wretches, whom they have so inhumanely and barbarously butcher'd and harass'd with several kinds of Torments, never before known, or heard (of which you shall have some account in the following Discourse) that of Three Millions of Persons, which lived in Hispaniola itself, there is at present but the inconsiderable remnant of scarce Three Hundred.
author: Bartolomé de las Casas
work: Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias (1552), English translation of 1689
witness: Las Casas, a former encomendero turned Dominican friar, wrote to move Charles V against the conquistadors; his figures (three million on Hispaniola) are rhetorical and far above modern estimates of a few hundred thousand. This 1689 London translation was published as anti-Catholic propaganda under the title "Popery Truly Display’d", one root of the Black Legend. The collapse he witnessed was real; the numbers are not a census.

name: Bernal Díaz sees Tenochtitlan for the first time
text: The next morning we reached the broad high road of Iztapalapan, whence we for the first time beheld the numbers of towns and villages built in the lake, and the still greater number of large townships on the mainland, with the level causeway which ran in a straight line into Mexico. Our astonishment was indeed raised to the highest pitch, and we could not help remarking to each other, that all these buildings resembled the fairy castles we read of in Amadis de Gaul; so high, majestic, and splendid did the temples, towers, and houses of the town, all built of massive stone and lime, rise up out of the midst of the lake. Indeed, many of our men believed what they saw was a mere dream.
author: Bernal Díaz del Castillo
work: True History of the Conquest of New Spain, tr. Lockhart (1844)
witness: Díaz wrote in old age in Guatemala, about fifty years after the events, partly to claim rewards and to correct Gómara’s Cortés-centred history. His wonder is literary (he reaches for a chivalric romance) and also strategic: the grander the city, the greater the conquerors.

name: Bernal Díaz on how smallpox reached Mexico
text: But to return to Narvaez. He happened to have a negro servant with him ill with the smallpox, through whom this terrific disease, which, according to the accounts of the inhabitants, was previously unknown in the country, spread itself through New Spain, where it created the greater devastation, from the poor Indians, in their ignorance, solely applying cold water as a remedy, with which they constantly bathed themselves; so that vast numbers were cut off
author: Bernal Díaz del Castillo
work: True History of the Conquest of New Spain, tr. Lockhart (1844)
witness: Written decades later from memory. Spanish sources pin the epidemic on one African man (named elsewhere as Francisco de Eguía); a single carrier is plausible, but the story also shifts blame away from the conquerors, and the remark about bathing reflects Spanish medical prejudice. Nahua accounts in the Florentine Codex describe the same epidemic from the victims’ side.

name: J. Theodore Bent claims foreign builders for Great Zimbabwe
text: From this mass of fresh evidence as to the curves and orientation of the Mashonaland ruins we may safely consider that the builders of these mysterious structures were well versed in geometry, and studied carefully the heavens. Beyond this nothing, of course, can really be proved until an enormous amount of careful study has been devoted to the subject. It is, however, very valuable confirmatory evidence when taken with the other points, that the builders were of a Semitic race and of Arabian origin, and quite excludes the possibility of any negroid race having had more to do with their construction than as the slaves of a race of higher cultivation; for it is a well-accepted fact that the negroid brain never could be capable of taking the initiative in work of such intricate nature.
author: J. Theodore Bent
work: The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland (3rd ed., 1895)
witness: Bent dug at Great Zimbabwe in 1891 with funding from Rhodes’ British South Africa Company and the Royal Geographical Society, a year after the company occupied Mashonaland. The racist conclusion here came first and the evidence was bent to it; every later excavation (Randall-MacIver 1905, Caton-Thompson 1929, Garlake, Chirikure) found the builders were Africans. Quoted as a witness to colonial ideology, not to the past.

name: Mungo Park watches Mande gold-washing
text: About the beginning of December, when the harvest is over and the streams and torrents have greatly subsided, the mansa or chief of the town appoints a day to begin sanoo koo (gold-washing), and the women are sure to have themselves in readiness by the time appointed. ... I have seen women who have had the skin worn off the tops of their fingers in this employment.
author: Mungo Park
work: Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa, ch. 21
witness: A Scottish surgeon travelling for the African Association, which wanted to open the interior to British trade; he spent months at Kamalia in 1797 waiting out the rains. He saw small-scale village gold-washing under a local mansa, four centuries after Mali’s height, so this shows how alluvial gold was worked, not the scale of the medieval trade.

name: Mungo Park on slavery inside West Africa
text: The slaves in Africa, I suppose, are nearly in the proportion of three to one to the freemen. They claim no reward for their services except food and clothing, and are treated with kindness or severity, according to the good or bad disposition of their masters.
author: Mungo Park
work: Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa, ch. 22
witness: Park’s three-to-one ratio is a guess from the Mande lands he crossed, not a count. His book appeared during the abolition debate, and its account of African slavery was used by both sides; his editor Bryan Edwards was a pro-slavery planter. Still, it is an early eyewitness of the internal slavery Lovejoy describes.

name: Cieza de León on the guayra furnaces of Potosí
text: The Indians, who were so ingenious, found that in some parts the silver could not be extracted with the aid of bellows, as was the case at Potosi. They, therefore, made certain moulds of clay, in the shape of a flower-pot in Spain, with many airholes in all parts. Charcoal was put into these moulds, with the metal on the top, and they were then placed on the part of the hill where the wind blew strongest, and thus the metal was extracted, which was then purified and refined with small bellows. In this manner all the metal that has been taken from the hill is extracted. The Indians go to the heights with the ores to extract the silver, and they call the moulds Guayras. ... As the Indians have no overseers when they carry the metal up to the heights, it must be supposed that they have enriched themselves, and taken much silver to their own homes.
author: Pedro de Cieza de León
work: Crónica del Perú, part 1, ch. 109, tr. Markham (1864)
witness: Cieza was a Spanish soldier-chronicler who saw Potosí in 1549 and published in Seville in 1553. He admired Andean skill and wrote before the mita and mercury amalgamation (1570s) transformed the mines, so this is the early, Indigenous-run boom. His remarks on Indians enriching themselves also echo colonists’ complaints about losing silver.

name: A British officer dines with Toussaint Louverture’s army
text: I then retired to the American hotel, and was introduced to the table d’ hote—to behold for the first time a perfect system of equality! Here were officers and privates, the general and the fifer, at the same table indiscriminately. I had the honour of sitting near a fat drummer, who very freely helped himself from my dish, and addressed me with frequent repetitions of “A votre Santé bon Americain.” Here also TOUSSAINT dined, but did not take the head of the table, from the idea (I was informed) that no man should be invested with superiority but in the field.
author: Marcus Rainsford
work: A Memoir of Transactions that Took Place in St. Domingo, in the Spring of 1799
witness: Rainsford, a British army captain, landed at Cap-Français in 1799 posing as an American and was later arrested as a spy. He published in 1802, as Leclerc sailed, partly to argue Toussaint was no threat to Britain’s islands. His admiration is genuine but filtered through British politics and a taste for the exotic.

name: A slave-ship captain estimates the yearly trade
text: Now, by these means it is that so many of the Negroes become Slaves, and more especially by being taken Captives in War. Of these the Number is so great, that I may safely affirm, without any Exaggeration, that the Europeans of all Nations, that trade to the Coast of Guinea, have, in some Years, exported at least seventy thousand.
author: William Snelgrave
work: A New Account of Some Parts of Guinea, and the Slave-Trade (1734)
witness: Snelgrave was an English slaving captain who wrote to defend the trade; the next pages argue it saved captives’ lives. His figure of 70,000 a year in some years is a merchant’s guess, but it is close to the voyage database’s totals for the early eighteenth century.

name: Roger Casement reports the emptying of the Congo
text: The natives certainly attribute their alarming death-rate to this as one of the inducing causes, although they attribute, and I think principally, their rapid decrease in numbers to other causes as well. Perhaps the most striking change observed during my journey into the interior was the great reduction observable everywhere in native life. Communities I had formerly known as large and flourishing centres of population are to-day entirely gone, or now exist in such diminished numbers as to be no longer recognizable.
author: Roger Casement
work: Report of the British Consul on the Congo (1904)
witness: A British consul’s official report to Parliament after a journey up the Congo in 1903, written amid a reform campaign and British commercial rivalry with Leopold. Casement compared what he saw with his own memories from the 1880s, and he gives sleeping sickness a real share of the blame alongside forced labour, which makes the report more credible, not less.

name: Columbus describes the Taíno to his sponsors
text: They have neither iron, nor steel, nor arms, nor are they competent to use them, not that they are not well-formed and of handsome stature, but because they are timid to a surprising degree. ... they are guileless, and so liberal of all they have that no one would believe it who had not seen it. ... so that the men I have left could, alone, destroy the whole country
author: Christopher Columbus
work: Letter to Luis de Santángel, February-March 1493, tr. R. H. Major
witness: Written on the return voyage to sell the enterprise to the crown and its financiers: gold, spices and gentle, defenceless people. Read it as a sales pitch and a statement of intent; the last line already imagines conquest.

name: Sarmiento on the capture of Huascar in the Inca civil war
text: Chalco Chima, searching for Huascar, saw him in his litter and seized him by the hands, and pulled him out of his litter. Thus was taken prisoner the unfortunate Huascar Inca, twelfth and last tyrant of the Inca Sovereigns of Peru, falling into the power of another greater and more cruel tyrant than himself, his people defeated, killed, and scattered.
author: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa
work: History of the Incas (1572), tr. Markham (1907)
witness: Written for Viceroy Toledo from interviews with Inca nobles in Cusco, and read back to them for approval, but with a purpose: to prove the Incas were recent tyrants so that Spain’s rule was legitimate. Hence "tyrant" on every page. The military narrative of the civil war is detailed and broadly matches other chronicles.

name: John Lloyd Stephens on who built the Maya cities
text: The conclusion to which I came was, that "there are not sufficient grounds for belief in the great antiquity that has been ascribed to these ruins;" "that we are not warranted in going back to any ancient nation of the Old World for the builders of these cities; that they are not the works of people who have passed away, and whose history is lost; but that there are strong reasons to believe them the creation of the same races who inhabited the country at the time of the Spanish conquest, or of some not very distant progenitors."
author: John Lloyd Stephens
work: Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. 1
witness: An American lawyer-diplomat and travel writer, quoting his own 1841 book, at a time when many writers credited the ruins to Egyptians, Israelites or lost races. Stephens was right that living Maya descended from the builders, a lesson Great Zimbabwe’s visitors ignored fifty years later. He also bought and shipped monuments away.
